For every $n\ge0$, the map
$\operatorname{enc}_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,\ldots,2^n-1\}$ of
[[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]] is a bijection. Any permutation of the
$n$ bit positions therefore induces a permutation of the corresponding
computational basis.

For $n\ge0$ and a binary word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})\in\{0,1\}^n$, define its
**big-endian index**

$$\operatorname{enc}_n(x):=\sum_{k<n}x_k\,2^{\,n-1-k}.$$

Thus the first wire is the most significant bit. For $n=0$, the domain
$\{0,1\}^0$ consists only of the empty word $()$, and the empty sum gives
$\operatorname{enc}_0(())=0$. In an ordered $n$-qubit
computational basis, the word $x$ occupies the slot numbered
$\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For an integer $N\ge1$, let $\mathcal F_N$ be the negative-sign, $N^{-1/2}$-normalized transform of [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]]. Define the **cyclic quantum Fourier transform** by $\operatorname{QFT}_N:=\mathcal F_N^{-1}$. The inverse exists by [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]], and its matrix on the standard basis indexed by $0,\ldots,N-1$ is

$$\operatorname{QFT}_N|x\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{y=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ixy/N}|y\rangle,\qquad 0\le x<N.$$

Here the standard-basis ket convention is the one specified by [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]]. Thus the transform has the positive sign and the same $N^{-1/2}$ normalization as the inverse Fourier formula. At $N=1$ it is the identity on the one-dimensional register. In the binary specialization $N=2^n$, the circuit page writes each index in its unique base-two expansion.

In the computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$, use $X,Y,Z$ from [[def-qc-pauli-matrices]] and define
$$H:=\frac{X+Z}{\sqrt2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix},\qquad T:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix}.$$
The phases displayed in these matrices are exact; they are not identified modulo a scalar when the matrices are later placed under a control.

For real $\theta$ and a real unit vector $\mathbf n=(n_x,n_y,n_z)$, define the axis rotation
$$R_{\mathbf n}(\theta):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i\theta}{2}\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\right),\qquad R_z(\theta):=R_{(0,0,1)}(\theta).$$
Here $\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ and $\|\mathbf n\|_2$ have the meanings fixed in [[def-qc-bloch-coordinate-map]]. For a bounded endomorphism $B$ of $Q_2$, the notation $\exp(B)$ means the operator-norm series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^k/k!$ of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]] at scalar parameter $1$. Its convergence applies here because $Q_2$ is finite-dimensional and complete and every linear endomorphism of $Q_2$ is bounded ([[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]], [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]]).

The unitary identities for the fixed matrices are verified below. The following theorem proves the closed form and unitarity of each $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$.

For a real angle $\theta$, define the one-qubit phase matrix $P_\theta=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\theta})$. In control-first order define

$$CP(\theta):=C(P_\theta)=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,e^{i\theta})$$

in the ordered basis $|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle$. This is the exact controlled phase; no circuit cost or controlled access to an arbitrary black-box unitary is implied.

derivations.claim: For $n\ge1$, bijectivity [F1] lets us index the output basis by all bit words $(y_{n-1},\ldots,y_0)$ in wire order; [F2] gives $y=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}y_j2^j$. Then $xy/2^n=\sum_j y_jx/2^{n-j}$. In the term indexed by $y_j$, put $k=n-1-j$. The fractional part of $x/2^{n-j}$ is $\sum_{i=0}^{k}x_i2^{-(k-i+1)}$: terms with $i>k$ are integers and the remaining powers have exactly these denominators. Thus the phase attached to output bit $y_j$ is the phase of $R_{n-1-j}$.

Consequently $e^{2\pi ixy/2^n}=\prod_j e^{2\pi iy_j\sum_{i=0}^{n-1-j}x_i2^{-(n-j-i)}}$. Summing over all bit strings $y$ factors as a tensor product of the two-term sums for the individual $y_j$; the normalization $2^{-n/2}$ is the product of the $n$ factors $2^{-1/2}$. By [F3], in wire order $q_{n-1},\ldots,q_0$ the factor sequence is $R_0\otimes\cdots\otimes R_{n-1}$, and [F4] identifies these coordinate factors with the corresponding kets.

In the descending-target circuit, the block on $q_j$ applies $H$ followed by $CP(2\pi/2^{j-i+1})$ from each control $q_i$ with $i<j$. Before this block, all lower wires are still in the basis states $|x_i\rangle$: previous blocks target only higher wires, and [F6] leaves basis controls unchanged. By [F5], the Hadamard contributes relative phase $(-1)^{x_j}=e^{2\pi i x_j/2}$; by [F6], the controlled phases multiply it by $\prod_{i<j}e^{2\pi i x_i/2^{j-i+1}}$. Thus the block prepares $R_j$ without changing the lower wires or previously prepared higher factors. Induction down the finite loop gives $R_{n-1}\otimes\cdots\otimes R_0$ before reversal. By [F3], reversal gives the output of step 2.1. At $n=0$, the loop is empty, $N=1$, and both states are the empty tensor $1$.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, the following are equivalent:

1. $T$ preserves norms.
2. $T$ preserves inner products.
3. $T$ sends every orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
4. $T$ sends some orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
5. $T^*T=I$.

Whenever these conditions hold, $T$ is invertible and $T^{-1}=T^*$, so also $TT^*=I$. The zero-dimensional case is included.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

If $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ is a finite orthonormal list and $v$ is any vector, then

$$\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2\le\lVert v\rVert^2.$$

Equality holds exactly when $v\in\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$. If the list is an orthonormal basis, then for all $v,w$,

$$v=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i,\qquad \langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle w,e_i\rangle},$$

and

$$\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2.$$

The empty-list case is included.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]].

derivations.claim: Fix any $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|=1$, and set $\alpha=U\psi$ and $\beta=\lambda V\psi$. By [F4], [F7] and $|\lambda|=1$, both vectors have norm $1$. Parseval [F6] makes their squared coordinate moduli nonnegative weights summing to $1$, so [F1] gives the output probability laws. For each $b\in B$, [F5] applied to $\alpha_b=(\alpha_b-\beta_b)+\beta_b$ and then to the reversed pair gives $\bigl||\alpha_b|-|\beta_b|\bigr|\le|\alpha_b-\beta_b|$. Factoring a difference of squares and applying [F2] gives $d_{\rm TV}(p_U^\psi,p_{\lambda V}^\psi)\le\tfrac12\|\alpha-\beta\|_2(\sum_b(|\alpha_b|+|\beta_b|)^2)^{1/2}$. Expanding the last squared sum and applying [F2] to the two nonnegative coordinate lists bounds its square root by $\|\alpha\|_2+\|\beta\|_2=2$, so the total variation is at most $\|\alpha-\beta\|_2$.

If $\gamma_b$ is the $b$-th coordinate of $V\psi$, then $\beta_b=\lambda\gamma_b$ and $|\beta_b|^2=|\lambda|^2|\gamma_b|^2=|\gamma_b|^2$ by modulus multiplicativity in [F5]. Hence $p_{\lambda V}^\psi=p_V^\psi$. Also $\|\alpha-\beta\|_2=\|(U-\lambda V)\psi\|_2\le\|U-\lambda V\|$ by [F3] and $\|\psi\|_2=1$. Combining with step 1.1 gives $d_{\rm TV}(p_U^\psi,p_V^\psi)\le\|U-\lambda V\|$ for every unit scalar $\lambda$.
Taking the infimum over all $|\lambda|=1$ in step 2.1 gives $d_{\rm TV}(p_U^\psi,p_V^\psi)\le d_{\rm pr}(U,V)\le\varepsilon$. No minimizing phase is required.

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces, with the product bases of
[[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For a permutation $\sigma$ of the
factor positions, the map $P_\sigma$ that reorders the factors is a bijective
linear isometry from $H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$ to
$H_{\sigma(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{\sigma(n-1)}$. When source and target
are identified as the same register, $P_\sigma$ is a unitary operator in the
sense of [[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]].

derivations.claim: Write the specified orthonormal bases as $f_0,\ldots,f_{a-1}$ for $S$ and $e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1}$ for $R$; $a,d\ge1$. By [F1], $f_k\otimes e_j$ form an orthonormal basis of $S\otimes R$. Expand $v=\sum_{k<a,j<d}c_{kj}f_k\otimes e_j$ and set $v_j=\sum_{k<a}c_{kj}f_k$. Grouping this finite sum gives $v=\sum_{j<d}v_j\otimes e_j$, while orthonormality gives $\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{j<d}\lVert v_j\rVert^2$. By [F2], $(T\otimes I_R)v=\sum_{j<d}Tv_j\otimes e_j$. Hence [F3] gives $\lVert(T\otimes I_R)v\rVert^2=\sum_{j<d}\lVert Tv_j\rVert^2\le\lVert T\rVert^2\sum_{j<d}\lVert v_j\rVert^2=\lVert T\rVert^2\lVert v\rVert^2$, so $\lVert T\otimes I_R\rVert\le\lVert T\rVert$.

Choose a unit vector $s\in S$ attaining the maximum in [F3], and choose a unit vector $e\in R$. The product inner product gives $\lVert s\otimes e\rVert=1$, and [F2] gives $\lVert(T\otimes I_R)(s\otimes e)\rVert=\lVert Ts\rVert=\lVert T\rVert$. Thus $\lVert T\otimes I_R\rVert\ge\lVert T\rVert$, proving the first equality.

If the tensor register is zero-dimensional, both $A$ and $PAP^{-1}$ have operator norm $0$ by [F3], proving the conjugation equality. Otherwise [F5] shows that $P$ and $P^{-1}$ preserve norms, so each has operator norm $1$ by [F3]. Submultiplicativity [F4] gives $\lVert PAP^{-1}\rVert\le\lVert A\rVert$. Applying the same inequality to $A=P^{-1}(PAP^{-1})P$ gives the reverse inequality. Therefore $\lVert PAP^{-1}\rVert=\lVert A\rVert$ in every case.

Let $n\ge0$, $N=2^n$, and take the input word $(x_{n-1},\ldots,x_0)$ in wire order $q_{n-1},\ldots,q_0$. By the big-endian index convention, its integer is $x=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_i2^i$, with $x_i\in\{0,1\}$. For $0\le j<n$, set

$$R_j:=2^{-1/2}\bigl(|0\rangle+e^{2\pi i\sum_{i=0}^{j}x_i2^{-(j-i+1)}}|1\rangle\bigr).$$

With the register order $q_{n-1},\ldots,q_0$, the standard-basis output $\operatorname{QFT}_{2^n}|x\rangle$ is $R_0\otimes R_1\otimes\cdots\otimes R_{n-1}$. The ordered factors immediately before the final wire-reversal permutation of the exact circuit are $R_{n-1}\otimes\cdots\otimes R_0$. For $n=0$, both are the empty tensor product, interpreted as the scalar $1$.

The **ideal binary-QFT gate-count model** treats each Hadamard $H$ and each exact controlled phase $\mathrm{CP}_s$ as one elementary gate, for integer $s\ge2$, where

Input: an $n$-qubit ordered register as in [[alg-qa-exact-binary-qft-circuit]] and an integer cutoff $m\ge1$.

Output: run the exact binary QFT circuit except omit every controlled phase $\mathrm{CP}_s$ with denominator index $s>m$. Retain every Hadamard and every final reversal SWAP. The resulting gate list is finite and unitary for every $n\ge0,m\ge1$ under [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]]. If $m\ge n$, no controlled phase is omitted and the circuit is exactly the full circuit. The ideal gate-count convention is [[def-qa-qft-gate-cost-model]].

The **ideal binary-QFT gate-count model** treats each Hadamard $H$ and each exact controlled phase $\mathrm{CP}_s$ as one elementary gate, for integer $s\ge2$, where

$$H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CP}_s=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,e^{2\pi i/2^s}).$$

A named SWAP, the wire permutation from [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]], counts as one two-qubit gate. If the implementation expands each SWAP into three exact CNOT gates of [[def-qc-cnot-and-control-target-order]], count those three CNOTs in place of that SWAP. These conventions refine the one-qubit alphabet, controlled-phase rotation and elementary circuit-resource interfaces of [[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]], [[def-qc-controlled-phase-rotation]] and [[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]].

The **finite-set synthesis model** keeps ideal gate count separate from compiled gate count. A one- or two-qubit target block is assigned a projective operator-error tolerance $\delta>0$; a scalar phase returned by the compiler is retained as metadata for the whole standalone circuit. Each CNOT expanded from a SWAP is exact in this model. Any compiled-count theorem must state the fixed-arity decomposition, finite alphabet, inverse-closure, density, exact-arithmetic and compiler-threshold hypotheses it uses. In particular, it makes no claim about classical bit-time for computing an arbitrary target-angle description. This is a cost convention; correctness and compiler resource bounds are separate theorems.

On two ordered qubit wires, let $S$ be the wire-swap permutation $|a,b\rangle\mapsto|b,a\rangle$. Let $C_{12}$ be the CNOT with wire 1 controlling wire 2, so $C_{12}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\oplus a\rangle$, and define the reverse orientation by $C_{21}|a,b\rangle=|a\oplus b,b\rangle$, extending both actions linearly; here $\oplus$ is addition modulo two. The operator identity

$$S=C_{12}C_{21}C_{12}$$

holds, where products act right to left. Therefore the swap of two wires has an exact three-CNOT implementation with no ancillas.

Let $n\ge1$, $N=2^n$, and let $m\ge1$ be an integer. For $1\le m<n$,

$$\|\operatorname{QFT}_{2^n}-\operatorname{QFT}^{(m)}_{2^n}\|\le\sum_{s=m+1}^{n}(n-s+1)\frac{2\pi}{2^s}\le2\pi n\,2^{-m}.$$

For $m\ge n$, the truncated circuit is exact and the error is zero. In particular, for $0<\varepsilon<1$, the cutoff $m=\min\{n,\lceil\log_2(2\pi n/\varepsilon)\rceil\}$ gives operator-norm error at most $\varepsilon$.

derivations.claim: For each target $q_j$, the exact circuit has $j$ controlled phases. A retained denominator level $s$ corresponds to pairs with $j-i+1=s$, namely $i=0,\ldots,n-s$, and so has $n-s+1$ gates. The cutoff retains precisely $s=2,\ldots,\widetilde m$. If $m\ge n$, then $\widetilde m=n$ and every phase is retained.

There are $n$ target wires, $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ final swaps, and no other gates or ancillas by [F1]. Summing their costs by [F2] gives the formula. Since $\sum_{s=2}^{\widetilde m}(n-s+1)\le n(\widetilde m-1)$ and $\lfloor n/2\rfloor\le n/2$, the total is at most $n\widetilde m+n/2$, hence $O(n\widetilde m+n)$. Under the cutoff in [F4] and $\varepsilon\ge n^{-c}$, $m\le\lceil\log_2(2\pi n^{c+1})\rceil=O_c(\log n)$, so $\widetilde m=O_c(\log n)$. The CNOT expansion is exact by [F3] and changes only the final reversal term; it does not compile any rotation.

Let $\mathcal H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space ([[def-inner-product-space]]) with a fixed orthonormal computational basis $B$ ([[def-orthogonal-vectors-sets-and-orthonormal-bases]]), and let $U,V:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$ be unitary operators, meaning invertible linear isometries ([[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]]). For a unit vector $\psi$, write $U\psi=\sum_{b\in B}\alpha_b|b\rangle$ and $V\psi=\sum_{b\in B}\beta_b|b\rangle$, and define their output laws by $p_U^\psi(b)=|\alpha_b|^2$ and $p_V^\psi(b)=|\beta_b|^2$. Unitarity and orthonormality make these finite probability laws ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]). For laws $p,q$ on $B$, define total variation by $d_{\rm TV}(p,q):=\tfrac12\sum_{b\in B}|p(b)-q(b)|$. Define projective operator distance by $d_{\rm pr}(U,V):=\inf_{|\lambda|=1}\|U-\lambda V\|$, where $\|\cdot\|$ is the operator norm. If $d_{\rm pr}(U,V)\le\varepsilon$ for $\varepsilon\ge0$, then

$$d_{\rm TV}(p_U^\psi,p_V^\psi)\le\varepsilon.$$

The same bound therefore holds for every computational-basis output law of the two operators. The proof verifies directly that multiplying a vector by a unit scalar leaves these coordinate probabilities unchanged.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, the following are equivalent:

1. $T$ preserves norms.
2. $T$ preserves inner products.
3. $T$ sends every orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
4. $T$ sends some orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
5. $T^*T=I$.

Whenever these conditions hold, $T$ is invertible and $T^{-1}=T^*$, so also $TT^*=I$. The zero-dimensional case is included.

**Inputs:** A fixed inverse-closed dense gate package $G$ with the finite
base-net certificate $(\mathcal N_0,\eta_0,L_0)$ from
[[def-qc-inverse-closed-dense-su2-gate-set]], an exact-real target
$U\in SU(2)$, and a rational $0<\varepsilon\le\eta_0$. This is an ideal
exact-real procedure: fixed-dimensional exact matrix arithmetic, matrix
logarithm/exponential, and exact comparisons are unit-cost operations. It is
not, by this definition alone, a finite Turing algorithm.

Set $\eta_{j+1}=64\eta_j^{3/2}$ for $j\ge0$. Choose the least integer
$J\ge0$ with $\eta_J\le\varepsilon$. Define $\operatorname{Compile}(U,j)$
recursively:

1. If $j=0$, return the first word $A\in\mathcal N_0$ with
   $\|U-A\|\le\eta_0$.
2. If $j>0$, set $A=\operatorname{Compile}(U,j-1)$ and $D=UA^*$.
   If $D=I$, set $V=W=I$. Otherwise apply the Pauli-coordinate construction
   in [[lem-qc-su2-balanced-commutator]] to $D$ and $\eta_{j-1}$, obtaining
   $V,W\in SU(2)$ with $D$ approximated by $VWV^*W^*$.
3. Set $B=\operatorname{Compile}(V,j-1)$ and
   $C=\operatorname{Compile}(W,j-1)$. Return the word
   $BCB^*C^*A$. Store concatenations and inverses as a shared expression DAG;
   an inverse word is formed by reversing its label order and replacing each
   label by its listed inverse. Expanding the DAG writes the ordinary gate word.

Return $\operatorname{Compile}(U,J)$. The recursion depth is finite because
each call decreases the nonnegative integer $j$.

For a fixed inverse-closed dense $G\subset SU(2)$ and a certified base net of
radius $0<\eta_0<64^{-2}$ and a target $U\in SU(2)$, the level recursion
$\operatorname{Compile}(U,J)$ of
[[alg-qc-solovay-kitaev-unitary-compiler]] returns, for every real
$0<\varepsilon\le\eta_0$, a word $W$ with
$\|U-W\|\le\varepsilon$, where $J$ is the least nonnegative integer
with $\eta_J\le\varepsilon$. For a real tolerance this means selecting
$J$ by ideal exact-real comparisons and calling the level subroutine
directly; the algorithm's top-level tolerance input is rational.
The level errors may be chosen as
$$\eta_j=64^{-2}(64^2\eta_0)^{(3/2)^j}.$$
The word length is at most $L_0 5^j$ at level $j$, hence
$O(\log^{\log_{3/2}5}(1/\varepsilon))=O(\log^{3.97}(1/\varepsilon))$.
With shared recursive words, the exact-real arithmetic count is
$O(\log^{\log_{3/2}3}(1/\varepsilon))=O(\log^{2.71}(1/\varepsilon))$;
printing the expanded word takes $O(\log^{3.97}(1/\varepsilon))$ time.
The latter are exact-real arithmetic bounds, not bit-complexity bounds.

Write $SU(2):=\{M\in M_2(\mathbb C):M^*M=I_2,\det M=1\}$. An
**inverse-closed dense $SU(2)$ gate package** consists of a finite set
$G\subset SU(2)$ of exact matrices with finite labels such that $g^{-1}=g^*$
belongs to $G$ for each $g\in G$ and the subgroup $\langle G\rangle$ of finite
products is dense in $SU(2)$ in operator norm. A word is a finite ordered list
of labels; its value is the corresponding matrix product, and its length is
the number of labels.

For a compiler package, also fix a rational $0<\eta_0<1/4096$, a finite list
$\mathcal N_0$ of words, and an integer $L_0$ such that every $U\in SU(2)$ is
within operator-norm distance $\eta_0/4$ of the value of some word in
$\mathcal N_0$, and every listed word has length at most $L_0$. This is a
finite **base-net certificate**. Density proves that such a certificate
exists, but does not compute the list or its maximum word length.

The orthogonal operators on a finite-dimensional real inner product space form a group under composition, as do the unitary operators on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space. Every such operator $T$ satisfies

$$|\det T|=1.$$

Over $\mathbb R$, this says $\det T\in\{-1,1\}$. In dimension zero, the unique determinant is $1$.

Every $z=a+bi\in\mathbb C$ has a square root. If $b\ne0$, one square root is
$$u+vi,\qquad u=\sqrt{\frac{|z|+a}{2}},\qquad v=\frac{b}{2u}.$$
If $b=0$, one may take $\sqrt a$ when $a\ge0$, and
$i\sqrt{-a}$ when $a<0$.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $S$ and $R$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with specified finite orthonormal bases, and let $T:S\to S$ be linear. With the product inner product on $S\otimes R$,

$$\lVert T\otimes I_R\rVert=\lVert T\rVert.$$

If $P$ is a unitary wire permutation on a finite ordered tensor register, then conjugating an endomorphism $A$ by $P$ preserves its operator norm: $\lVert PAP^{-1}\rVert=\lVert A\rVert$. Thus a one- or two-register gate has the same operator norm after identity factors are added on spectators and its wires are moved to their declared positions.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

On two ordered qubit wires, let $S$ be the wire-swap permutation $|a,b\rangle\mapsto|b,a\rangle$. Let $C_{12}$ be the CNOT with wire 1 controlling wire 2, so $C_{12}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\oplus a\rangle$, and define the reverse orientation by $C_{21}|a,b\rangle=|a\oplus b,b\rangle$, extending both actions linearly; here $\oplus$ is addition modulo two. The operator identity

$$S=C_{12}C_{21}C_{12}$$

holds, where products act right to left. Therefore the swap of two wires has an exact three-CNOT implementation with no ancillas.

Let $n\ge r\ge1$, let $w=(w_0,\ldots,w_{r-1})$ be an ordered tuple of distinct wires in $[n]$, and let $U:\mathcal Q_r\to\mathcal Q_r$ be unitary. There is a unique unitary $\widetilde U_w:\mathcal Q_n\to\mathcal Q_n$ that applies $U$ to the ordered wires $w_0,\ldots,w_{r-1}$ and acts as the identity on the other wires.

For every $U\in U(2)$, the exact controlled matrix $C(U)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,U)$ is realized with two CNOTs and one-qubit gates only. The scalar phase of $U$ is implemented as a phase gate on the control and is not discarded.

For a real angle $\theta$, define the one-qubit phase matrix $P_\theta=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\theta})$. In control-first order define

$$CP(\theta):=C(P_\theta)=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,e^{i\theta})$$

in the ordered basis $|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle$. This is the exact controlled phase; no circuit cost or controlled access to an arbitrary black-box unitary is implied.

Fix a finite gate alphabet $G$ with maximum arity $k:=\max(\{r(g):g\in G\}\cup\{0\})$ and a circuit from [[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]]. The declared **size** is the number of gate occurrences, equivalently $\sum_{t=1}^d|L_t|$; the declared **depth** is the number $d$ of explicit layers, not a minimum over alternate layerings; the **width** is the number $n$ of all wires, including workspace wires. The operation model may also assign weighted gate costs, classical bit costs, and query costs; these are separate coordinates and are summed over the calls actually made.

A workspace wire is an ancilla. A **clean-ancilla promise** specifies computational-basis zero states for the ancillas and requires their exact return for every allowed data input: if $U$ is the implemented unitary, $V_D$ is the declared data unitary, and $|0_A\rangle$ is the specified joint zero vector, then $U(x\otimes|0_A\rangle)=V_Dx\otimes|0_A\rangle$ for every allowed data vector $x$. A **dirty-ancilla promise** permits an arbitrary ancilla state independent of the data input; it may be correlated with an untouched reference. Exact dirty-ancilla restoration means the implemented unitary on data and ancillas is $V_D\otimes I_A$ on the entire joint space, where $V_D$ is the declared unitary on data. The same operator equality then holds after tensoring with the identity on any finite untouched reference. Consequently, product input between the data and the combined ancilla/reference system remains product after the operation. No uncorrelated-output claim is made for an initially data-correlated ancilla.

A controlled or inverse operation is counted only when the operation model explicitly grants that access or supplies a construction; its charge is recorded separately from an ordinary call. Inverse availability and query or gate charges are also recorded separately from controlled forward access. In particular, the matrix of $U$ alone supplies neither a controlled call nor an inverse query, in accordance with [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]] and [[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]].

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and $U:H\to H$ a unitary. Let $\theta\in\mathbb R$, and suppose the model separately grants controlled access to both $U$ and $e^{i\theta}U$. There is a normalized eigenvector $\phi$ with $U\phi=\mu\phi$ and $|\mu|=1$. Let $C=Q_2=\mathbb C^2$ be the control qubit with ordered computational basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$; define $|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and prepare $(|0\rangle+\overline\mu|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ with target $\phi$. The two joint effects are $E_\pm=|\pm\rangle\langle\pm|\otimes I_H$. The $E_+$ outcome has probability $1$ after $C(U)$ and $\cos^2(\theta/2)$ after $C(e^{i\theta}U)$. Thus the two controlled maps give different outcome laws exactly when $\theta\notin2\pi\mathbb Z$; when $\theta\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, the controlled maps coincide. This is a mathematical witness; it does not assert that controlled access or the witness-state preparation is free.

derivations.claim: If $m<n$, then $2^m\ge4\pi n/\eta$, so [F2] gives truncation error at most $\eta/2$. If $m=n$, the truncated circuit is exact by [F2]. Thus in either case the ideal truncated unitary is within $\eta/2$ of the exact QFT.

There are $L$ retained one- or two-qubit blocks. For $m\ge1$, each summand in $L$ is at most $n$, hence $L\le n+n(m-1)=nm$. The final reversal uses $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ swaps, or $3\lfloor n/2\rfloor=O(n)$ exact CNOTs by [F15] and the resource convention [A2].

For any factor $U\in U(2)$, [F10] gives $|\det U|=1$. Choose $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $\lambda^2=\det U$ by [F11]. Then [F12] gives $|\lambda|^2=|\det U|=1$, so $|\lambda|=1$. The matrix $S=\lambda^{-1}U$ is unitary and has determinant $1$, hence $S\in SU(2)$. By [F7]–[F9] and $0<\delta\le\kappa\le\eta_0$, compile $S$ to a word $W$ with $\|S-W\|\le\delta$ and $O(\log^{3.97}(1/\delta))$ gates. Thus $\|U-\lambda W\|\le\delta$. The local error lifts to the full register with the same operator norm by [F13]. By [F14], the embedded scalar $\lambda$ remains one scalar on the entire standalone circuit.

Apply [A1] to each retained block: use one gate for a Hadamard and, for $C(P_\theta)$, the three target gates $A,B,C$ and one control phase gate from the controlled-unitary proof, with its two exact CNOTs. The phase gate is retained, so this is the complete controlled phase. These lists prove the uniform bound with $c=4$, independently of the angle. For any chosen lists bounded by $c$ as in the statement, the total number $K$ of one-qubit factors obeys $K\le cL$, and at most $cL$ CNOTs occur. Keep the Hadamards as one-gate lists, so $K\ge n\ge1$. No ancilla or unproved QSD optimization is used.

By the circuit denotation interface [A3], compose the compiled factors in chronological order, leaving every decomposition CNOT exact. The global embeddings act on their specified wires by [F16]. The exact-minus-compiled product telescopes with one local difference per one-qubit factor. Every surrounding factor is unitary and has norm one by [F6]; [F5] bounds the norm of the sum by the sum of local errors, at most $K\delta\le cL\delta\le\eta/2$. The product of the $K$ scalars from step 1.3 is one scalar for the whole standalone circuit.

Let $C$ be the compiled circuit and let $\lambda$ be the total scalar from step 3.1. The triangle inequality, step 1.1 and step 3.1 give $\|\operatorname{QFT}_{2^n}-\lambda C\|\le\eta$. By the max-over-unit-vectors definition in [F5], operator-norm homogeneity gives $\|C-\overline\lambda\operatorname{QFT}_{2^n}\|=\|\overline\lambda(\operatorname{QFT}_{2^n}-\lambda C)\|=\|\operatorname{QFT}_{2^n}-\lambda C\|\le\eta$; the first vectors differ by the scalar $-1$, and $|\lambda|=1$. Choosing $\overline\lambda$ in the defining infimum proves $d_{\rm pr}(C,\operatorname{QFT}_{2^n})\le\eta$. Applying [F4] gives the asserted total-variation bound for every unit input.

The scalar in step 3.1 is harmless for this standalone output law because the conclusion uses projective distance and [F4]. It cannot be silently discarded if this entire compiled block is placed under outer control, by [A4]; no outer-controlled compilation claim is made.

By [F8], the $K\le cL$ compiled one-qubit factors use $O(cL\log^{3.97}(1/\delta))$ gates. The decomposition CNOTs contribute at most $cL$ and the final SWAP expansion contributes $3\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ exact CNOTs by [A2,F15]. Since $L\le nm$ and $1/\delta=\max\{2cL/\eta,1/\kappa\}$ with fixed $c,\kappa$, $\log(1/\delta)=O(\log(2nm/\eta))$. Therefore the total is $O(nm\log^{3.97}(2nm/\eta))$. No step bounds the classical bit-time for target-angle descriptions.

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, the following are equivalent:

1. $T$ preserves norms.
2. $T$ preserves inner products.
3. $T$ sends every orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
4. $T$ sends some orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
5. $T^*T=I$.

Whenever these conditions hold, $T$ is invertible and $T^{-1}=T^*$, so also $TT^*=I$. The zero-dimensional case is included.
For every real $\theta$, $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

Let $n\ge1$, $N=2^n$, and let $m\ge1$ be an integer. For $1\le m<n$,

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Euler's formula and the quarter-turn values [F6,F7] give $e^{i\pi/2}=i$, $e^{i\pi}=-1$, and $e^{3\pi i/2}=-i$. For the nonnegative integer $xy$, iterating [F12] gives $e^{\pi ixy/2}=(e^{i\pi/2})^{xy}=i^{xy}$, with both sides $1$ when $xy=0$. After the final swap the factors are ordered as the $q_0$ factor followed by the $q_1$ factor. Substituting $x_1x_0=00,01,10,11$ gives the four columns $[1,1,1,1]^T$, $[1,i,-1,-i]^T$, $[1,-1,1,-1]^T$, and $[1,-i,-1,i]^T$, each divided by $2$; these are the amplitudes in [L3].

By [L2,A1], the difference of exact and cutoff operators is $S H(q_0)(\mathrm{CP}_2-I)H(q_1)$, where the left and right factors are unitary: $H^*H=I$, $\mathrm{CP}_2$ is diagonal with unit-modulus entries, and $S$ permutes an orthonormal basis [L1,F5,F9,F10]. Write a unit vector as $v=\sum_{a,b\in\{0,1\}}c_{ab}|ab\rangle$. By [F10], $\sum_{a,b}|c_{ab}|^2=1$. Hence $\|(\mathrm{CP}_2-I)v\|^2=2|c_{11}|^2\le2$, with equality at $v=|11\rangle$; [F8] gives $\|\mathrm{CP}_2-I\|=\sqrt2$. For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].
For $0<x\le2$, $\sin x\ge x-x^3/6\ge x/3>0$. Also $\cos2\le-1/3$. Consequently $\cos$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,2]$.

Let $(\varepsilon_k)$ be the alternating sequence of [[lem-alternating-sequence]],
that is the unique sequence of reals with $\varepsilon_0 = 1$ and
$\varepsilon_{k+1} = -\varepsilon_k$, which is what is usually written
$\varepsilon_k = (-1)^k$; let $e$ and $o$ be its even and odd index maps, so that
$\varepsilon_{e_j} = 1$, $\varepsilon_{o_j} = -1$, and every natural number is
$e_j$ for exactly one $j$ or $o_j$ for exactly one $j$.

Let $(b_k)$ be a sequence of reals that is nonincreasing
([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and converges to $0$ ([[def-real-limit]]); then
$b_k \ge 0$ for every $k$. Write $t_n := \sum_{k<n} \varepsilon_k b_k$ for the
partial sums ([[def-series]]). Then:

1. the series $\sum \varepsilon_k b_k$ converges; write $L$ for its sum;
2. $t_{e_j} \le L \le t_{o_j}$ for every $j \in \mathbb{N}$, and for every
   $n \in \mathbb{N}$ the sum $L$ lies between the two consecutive partial sums
   $t_n$ and $t_{n+1}$;
3. $|L - t_n| \le b_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Claim 3 is the error bound: the partial sum $t_n$, which uses the $n$ terms
$\varepsilon_0 b_0, \dots, \varepsilon_{n-1}b_{n-1}$, differs from the sum by at
most the first term omitted.

**Only claim 1 is a corollary of [[thm-dirichlet-test]].** Claims 2 and 3 are not:
they come from the interlacing of the even-index and odd-index partial sums, and
that argument is carried out below rather than smuggled into the Dirichlet
estimate, which produces no bracketing at all.
